pages.text: Student Representative Council elections were coming. Two candidates stood for president: Georgina and Sedem. Sedem’s posters said, “Vote Sedem: Free Sweets and Longer Break!” He handed out sweets at the gate. Students cheered. Georgina’s poster was plainer: “Vote Georgina: Listening, Planning, Delivering.” Her friend Ishmael groaned. “You cannot beat sweets with listening.”

Two candidates stood for president: Georgina and Sedem.

Students cheered.
Georgina’s poster was plainer: “Vote Georgina: Listening, Planning, Delivering.” Her friend Ishmael groaned.
“You cannot beat sweets with listening.”
pages.alt: Two campaign posters side by side on a wall, one with sweets and one plain.

pages.text: But Georgina had a plan. She went from class to class with a notebook, asking, “What is your biggest problem at school?” Students told her: broken taps, a dirty toilet block, no library hours after break, bullying at the gate. She wrote it all down. “A leader’s first job,” she told Ishmael, “is to listen. Then to promise only what she can deliver.”

She went from class to class with a notebook, asking, “What is your biggest problem at school?” Students told her: broken taps, a dirty toilet block, no library hours after break, bullying at the gate.
She wrote it all down.
“A leader’s first job,” she told Ishmael, “is to listen.
Then to promise only what she can deliver.”
pages.alt: A girl with a notebook talks to students in a classroom and writes down their problems.

pages.text: At the campaign rally, Sedem promised longer breaks, free sweets and no homework on Fridays. The crowd cheered. Georgina’s turn came. “I cannot promise you free sweets,” she said. “The SRC does not own sweets, and it does not decide the timetable. But I can promise to take your list of problems to the head teacher every month and to report back to you.” Some students clapped, some looked unsure.

pages.alt: A girl speaks at a microphone to a crowd while a boy waits with a bag of sweets.

pages.text: Mr Gbeku, the electoral officer, reminded the students of the rules before polling day. “Every student votes once. No campaigning at the ballot box. No bribery, and sweets for votes count as bribery. The secret ballot means nobody has to tell anyone how they voted.” Sedem blushed and put away his bag. “I did not mean it as a bribe,” he muttered. “It is a lesson for all of us,” said Mr Gbeku.

pages.alt: An electoral officer addresses students beside a ballot box and a list of rules.

pages.text: Polling day came. Students queued, signed the register and dropped their folded papers into the box. The count was done in public. Georgina won by forty-two votes. She shook Sedem’s hand. “Thank you for a fair contest,” she said. “Will you chair the Sports Committee?” Sedem was surprised, then grinned. “I would be honoured,” he said.

pages.text: In her first month, Georgina took the broken-taps list to the head teacher, who arranged repairs. The SRC held a clean-up day. The library stayed open for twenty extra minutes after break. Not every promise was kept at once, and Georgina said so honestly at the next assembly. “We fixed three of the five problems,” she reported. “We will keep working on the rest.” Students listened, because she told the truth.

pages.text: Georgina wrote to Madam Okyere, the head teacher, in full formal layout. In the top right corner she put her address, SRC Office, Hillview Basic School, Box 22, Koforidua, and beneath it the date, 3rd March, 2027. On the left she wrote the receiver’s designation and address: The Head Teacher, Hillview Basic School, Box 22, Koforidua. Next came the salutation, “Dear Madam,” and the heading, REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO HOLD A CLEAN-UP DAY. Her body read: “I am writing on behalf of the Student Representative Council to request your permission to hold a clean-up day on Saturday, 13th March. Firstly, litter on the compound can attract pests and harm our health. Secondly, we have prepared a list of forty volunteers, and a local Assembly member has offered to lend us tools. We shall be grateful for your approval.” She ended with “Yours faithfully,” her signature, and her full name, Georgina Amoah, SRC President.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a letter to a head teacher is formal, so it needs all eight features: the writer’s address, the date, the receiver’s designation and full address, “Dear Madam” or “Dear Sir”, a heading, “Yours faithfully”, a signature and the writer’s full name. The body should be polite, clear and persuasive, with reasons, and it must not use contractions, slang or chat words. In an exam, check who the reader is first. The end.
